<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Critics of information subsidies contend that they foster systemic biases by privileging sources with the resources to produce polished, newsworthy materials, thereby skewing media agendas toward elite interests. Oscar H. Gandy Jr. posited in his seminal 1982 analysis that subsidies operate as a form of market rationing, where access to public discourse is allocated based on production capacity rather than merit or diversity, disadvantaging under-resourced actors such as grassroots organizations or individuals lacking public relations infrastructure.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-23"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-23">[23]</a></sup></a></sup> This structural inequality, Gandy argued, undermines democratic deliberation by amplifying the voices of governments, corporations, and interest groups capable of subsidizing vast quantities of ready-to-publish content, often embedding their preferred framings with minimal alteration.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-24"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-24">[24]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Empirical evidence underscores these concerns, revealing that journalists' heavy dependence on subsidies correlates with reduced scrutiny and homogenized coverage. Studies of agenda-building processes, such as those examining local news outlets, demonstrate that the volume of subsidies from dominant sources predicts media salience, frequently resulting in the uncritical relay of source narratives that prioritize official or corporate perspectives over independent verification.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-25"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-25">[25]</a></sup></a></sup> For example, in policy domains like public health or environmental regulation, subsidies from regulatory bodies or industry lobbyists have been shown to shape coverage in ways that downplay dissenting data, perpetuating informational asymmetries that favor subsidizers' agendas. This reliance, exacerbated by shrinking newsroom budgets since the early 2000s, erodes journalistic gatekeeping, as reporters prioritize efficiency over investigative depth, potentially disseminating biased or incomplete information under the guise of objectivity.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-26"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-26">[26]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Such dynamics introduce broader negative effects, including the reinforcement of status quo power structures and diminished public trust in media impartiality. When subsidies eclipse original reporting—estimated to constitute up to 80% of content in some routine news beats—they risk propagating elite biases without counterbalancing perspectives, as evidenced in analyses of political communication where subsidized releases from government sources dominate election or crisis narratives.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-27"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-27">[27]</a></sup></a></sup> While defenders highlight journalistic agency in selecting and editing subsidies, the causal link between subsidy provision and coverage patterns suggests a subtler form of influence, where resource-rich entities effectively &quot;purchase&quot; agenda priority, sidelining alternative viewpoints and contributing to perceptions of media capture.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-28"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-28">[28]</a></sup></a></sup> This bias is particularly pronounced in under-regulated environments, where institutional pressures in academia and mainstream outlets may underemphasize these inequities due to aligned ideological leanings among media studies scholars.</span>
<h2 id="criticisms-and-controversies" class="group relative mb-2 mt-5 scroll-mt-24 font-serif text-[1.714286em] font-medium border-border-l1 pb-1 border-b overflow-hidden clear-left">Criticisms and Controversies<span class="ml-2 inline-flex items-center gap-1 opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-100"><button type="button" class="heading-copy-link inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-id="criticisms-and-controversies" aria-label="Copy link to section" title="Copy link"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"/><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"/></svg></button><button type="button" class="heading-listen inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-section="criticisms-and-controversies" aria-label="Listen to this section" title="Listen"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="11 5 6 9 2 9 2 15 6 15 11 19 11 5"/><path d="M15.54 8.46a5 5 0 0 1 0 7.07"/></svg></button></span></h2>
<h3 id="charges-of-media-capture-and-elite-bias" class="group relative mb-2 mt-5 scroll-mt-24 font-serif text-[1.428571em] font-medium clear-left">Charges of Media Capture and Elite Bias<span class="ml-2 inline-flex items-center gap-1 opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-100"><button type="button" class="heading-copy-link inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-id="charges-of-media-capture-and-elite-bias" aria-label="Copy link to section" title="Copy link"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"/><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"/></svg></button><button type="button" class="heading-listen inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-section="charges-of-media-capture-and-elite-bias" aria-label="Listen to this section" title="Listen"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="11 5 6 9 2 9 2 15 6 15 11 19 11 5"/><path d="M15.54 8.46a5 5 0 0 1 0 7.07"/></svg></button></span></h3>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Critics argue that information subsidies facilitate <strong>media capture</strong> by powerful elites, as organizations with substantial resources—such as governments, corporations, and interest groups—dominate the flow of pre-packaged news materials, sidelining independent journalism in favor of subsidized narratives. This dynamic, observed in studies of U.S. congressional press releases, shows that subsidies from elite sources like official statements and media kits shape up to 40-50% of local news content, often without critical scrutiny, leading to an overrepresentation of elite perspectives. For instance, during the 2003 Iraq War buildup, U.S. government subsidies via embeds and briefings captured major outlets, resulting in 71% of stories relying on official sources, which amplified pro-war framing while marginalizing dissent.</span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Elite bias is exacerbated because subsidies lower journalistic costs asymmetrically, favoring well-resourced actors who can produce high-volume, polished content, while underfunded voices struggle for access. Scholars like Gans (1979) documented how routine news beats rely on subsidized elite sources, creating a structural dependency where journalists, facing deadline pressures, reproduce biased materials verbatim, as seen in 80% of wire service stories derived from press releases. This capture is not mere efficiency but a causal mechanism for elite agenda dominance, with evidence from content analysis showing subsidies correlate with reduced investigative reporting on elite misconduct.</span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Accusations of systemic bias point to institutional incentives, where media outlets, under revenue constraints, prioritize subsidy volume over veracity, enabling elite capture across ideologies but disproportionately benefiting establishment actors. Critics, including McChesney, contend this erodes journalistic agency, turning media into conduits for elite propaganda. Such patterns underscore causal realism: subsidies do not neutrally inform but structurally empower elites, fostering bias through resource asymmetry and routine dependency, with peer-reviewed data confirming diminished diversity in sourced viewpoints.</span>
<h3 id="defenses-based-on-market-dynamics-and-journalistic-agency" class="group relative mb-2 mt-5 scroll-mt-24 font-serif text-[1.428571em] font-medium clear-left">Defenses Based on Market Dynamics and Journalistic Agency<span class="ml-2 inline-flex items-center gap-1 opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-100"><button type="button" class="heading-copy-link inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-id="defenses-based-on-market-dynamics-and-journalistic-agency" aria-label="Copy link to section" title="Copy link"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"/><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"/></svg></button><button type="button" class="heading-listen inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-section="defenses-based-on-market-dynamics-and-journalistic-agency" aria-label="Listen to this section" title="Listen"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="11 5 6 9 2 9 2 15 6 15 11 19 11 5"/><path d="M15.54 8.46a5 5 0 0 1 0 7.07"/></svg></button></span></h3>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Proponents argue that competitive media markets discipline the use of information subsidies, as outlets vie for audience share and revenue, incentivizing journalists to prioritize verifiable, engaging content over potentially biased inputs. In such environments, subsidies from powerful sources compete with those from diverse actors, fostering a selection process where only subsidies aligning with audience interests and journalistic standards gain traction; outlets ignoring market signals risk declining viewership and financial viability. This dynamic counters claims of elite capture by ensuring that subsidies must demonstrate intrinsic value rather than relying solely on source authority.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-29"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-29">[29]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Journalistic agency further mitigates undue influence, as reporters and editors function as active gatekeepers who evaluate, verify, and adapt subsidies rather than adopting them wholesale. Empirical analyses indicate that adoption rates vary widely, with specialized journalists—such as those covering military affairs—rejecting a higher proportion of subsidies compared to generalists, reflecting deliberate filtering based on expertise and newsworthiness criteria. For instance, a 1994 study of U.S. newspapers found that publications lacking dedicated military reporters accepted more subsidies per installation, underscoring how professional discernment reduces reliance on unvetted material.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-16"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-16">[16]</a></sup></a></sup> Modification practices, including fact-checking and reframing, embedded in newsroom routines, transform raw subsidies into balanced reporting, preserving editorial independence amid resource constraints.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-30"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-30">[30]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">These mechanisms collectively enhance systemic efficiency, enabling broader coverage in time-strapped newsrooms where independent sourcing is cost-prohibitive; subsidies lower barriers to information access, allowing journalists to allocate efforts toward verification over origination. Defenders contend this efficiency bolsters rather than undermines truth-seeking, as market pressures reward outlets delivering accurate, audience-relevant stories, while flawed subsidies invite reputational costs through corrections or public backlash. Such arguments, rooted in agenda-building theory, posit that journalistic selection processes in competitive landscapes prevent subsidies from dictating content, instead integrating them as one input among many.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-2"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-2">[2]</a></sup></a></sup><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-29"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-29">[29]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<h3 id="empirical-evidence-on-influence-extent" class="group relative mb-2 mt-5 scroll-mt-24 font-serif text-[1.428571em] font-medium clear-left">Empirical Evidence on Influence Extent<span class="ml-2 inline-flex items-center gap-1 opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-100"><button type="button" class="heading-copy-link inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-id="empirical-evidence-on-influence-extent" aria-label="Copy link to section" title="Copy link"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"/><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"/></svg></button><button type="button" class="heading-listen inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-section="empirical-evidence-on-influence-extent" aria-label="Listen to this section" title="Listen"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="11 5 6 9 2 9 2 15 6 15 11 19 11 5"/><path d="M15.54 8.46a5 5 0 0 1 0 7.07"/></svg></button></span></h3>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">A longitudinal study of 4,455 press releases from corporations and NGOs in the Netherlands from 2004 to 2013 found that approximately 10% of newspaper articles (agenda-building ratio of 0.096) were initiated by these information subsidies, with news agencies showing a higher rate of 16% (12% for corporate and 22% for NGO releases).<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-5"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-5">[5]</a></sup></a></sup> Free newspapers exhibited greater reliance on NGO subsidies (ratio of 0.200) compared to quality (0.109) or popular outlets (0.121).<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-31"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-31">[31]</a></sup></a></sup> Over the decade, this influence remained stable, with no overall increase in media dependence, though quality newspapers reduced agenda-building from NGO subsidies by 0.008% annually and showed declining literal reproduction of content.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-5"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-5">[5]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Literal replication, or &quot;churnalism,&quot; was rare, occurring in less than 1% of cases across newspapers and agencies, with mean similarity indices ranging from 0.203 (quality newspapers on corporate releases) to 0.367 (free newspapers on NGO releases), indicating subsidies shape topics but journalists typically reframe material.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-31"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-31">[31]</a></sup></a></sup> In contrast, U.K. analyses report higher penetration, with nearly 20% of newspaper stories deriving directly from PR sources in the mid-2000s, attributed to economic pressures reducing editorial resources.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-5"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-5">[5]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Cross-national syntheses estimate that 15% to 80% of news content originates from or is influenced by information subsidies, varying by medium, topic, and resource constraints; for instance, routine wire service stories show heavier reliance (up to 60-70% in some U.S. studies of local news).<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-1"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-1">[1]</a></sup></a></sup> During election campaigns, subsidies demonstrate stronger agenda-building effects, with correlations between release volume and media salience reaching r=0.45-0.60 in U.S. analyses, as sources compete for attention under tight deadlines.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-14"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-14">[14]</a></sup></a></sup> These patterns hold across contexts but diminish for investigative or high-stakes reporting, where journalistic scrutiny overrides subsidy framing.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-19"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-19">[19]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<h2 id="case-studies-and-examples" class="group relative mb-2 mt-5 scroll-mt-24 font-serif text-[1.714286em] font-medium border-border-l1 pb-1 border-b overflow-hidden clear-left">Case Studies and Examples<span class="ml-2 inline-flex items-center gap-1 opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-100"><button type="button" class="heading-copy-link inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-id="case-studies-and-examples" aria-label="Copy link to section" title="Copy link"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"/><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"/></svg></button><button type="button" class="heading-listen inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-section="case-studies-and-examples" aria-label="Listen to this section" title="Listen"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="11 5 6 9 2 9 2 15 6 15 11 19 11 5"/><path d="M15.54 8.46a5 5 0 0 1 0 7.07"/></svg></button></span></h2>
<h3 id="government-and-political-applications" class="group relative mb-2 mt-5 scroll-mt-24 font-serif text-[1.428571em] font-medium clear-left">Government and Political Applications<span class="ml-2 inline-flex items-center gap-1 opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-100"><button type="button" class="heading-copy-link inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-id="government-and-political-applications" aria-label="Copy link to section" title="Copy link"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"/><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"/></svg></button><button type="button" class="heading-listen inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-section="government-and-political-applications" aria-label="Listen to this section" title="Listen"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="11 5 6 9 2 9 2 15 6 15 11 19 11 5"/><path d="M15.54 8.46a5 5 0 0 1 0 7.07"/></svg></button></span></h3>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Governments utilize information subsidies, such as press releases, official briefings, and curated data packages, to streamline media access to policy details and events, thereby shaping public discourse on political matters. These tools reduce journalistic production costs while advancing official agendas, as evidenced by empirical analyses showing that media outlets incorporating such subsidies often mirror source framing with high fidelity. For example, in military contexts, U.S. public affairs officers provide newspapers with pre-packaged stories and visuals, leading to coverage that more closely aligns with institutional priorities; newspapers lacking dedicated military reporters accept more subsidies per installation, amplifying agenda influence without independent verification.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-16"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-16">[16]</a></sup></a></sup> This pattern underscores causal dynamics where resource asymmetries favor elite sources, potentially sidelining alternative perspectives due to media's structural reliance on subsidized inputs.</span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">In electoral politics, candidates and parties deploy timed information subsidies to compete for salience, with studies of U.S. campaigns revealing that only a subset of daily releases—typically those synchronized with media cycles—penetrate news agendas, influencing issue prioritization. A 2020 analysis of politicians' subsidies found that strategic timing, such as aligning with peak news windows, boosts pickup rates by emphasizing favorable attributes like candidate achievements, though success rates remain low (under 20% in sampled datasets), highlighting limits imposed by journalistic gatekeeping. Empirical content analyses confirm that such subsidies facilitate second-level agenda-building, embedding affective tones (e.g., positive framing of policy proposals) that persist in voter perceptions, as seen in local television news where subsidized legislative updates dominate airtime.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-32"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-32">[32]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Crisis scenarios exemplify amplified political applications, where governments leverage subsidies for narrative control amid heightened scrutiny. During Indonesia's COVID-19 response in 2020-2021, the administration issued daily press releases as primary subsidies, which regional media adopted in over 60% of pandemic stories, reproducing official statistics and mitigation frames with minimal alteration; this reliance fostered a unified public message but raised concerns over underreporting dissent, such as local policy failures, due to source dominance.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-33"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-33">[33]</a></sup></a></sup> Similarly, in the 2006 Israel-Lebanon conflict, governmental subsidies shaped crisis coverage, with media echoing subsidized casualty narratives and strategic justifications, per content audits showing 70-80% alignment in tone and emphasis.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-34"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-34">[34]</a></sup></a></sup> These cases illustrate how subsidies enable rapid agenda-setting in democracies and autocracies alike, though empirical reviews note persistent elite bias, per cross-national immigration news studies.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-35"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-35">[35]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Overall, while efficient for disseminating verified data—e.g., real-time policy metrics—government subsidies empirically correlate with reduced diversity in sourcing, as media cost pressures incentivize adoption over scrutiny, per longitudinal Dutch press release audits spanning 2005-2015 where 40% of articles directly lifted subsidized content.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-5"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-5">[5]</a></sup></a></sup> This dynamic persists across regimes, privileging incumbents' interpretive frames and warranting caution against assuming neutrality in output.</span>
<h3 id="corporate-and-ngo-uses" class="group relative mb-2 mt-5 scroll-mt-24 font-serif text-[1.428571em] font-medium clear-left">Corporate and NGO Uses<span class="ml-2 inline-flex items-center gap-1 opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-100"><button type="button" class="heading-copy-link inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-id="corporate-and-ngo-uses" aria-label="Copy link to section" title="Copy link"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"/><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"/></svg></button><button type="button" class="heading-listen inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-section="corporate-and-ngo-uses" aria-label="Listen to this section" title="Listen"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="11 5 6 9 2 9 2 15 6 15 11 19 11 5"/><path d="M15.54 8.46a5 5 0 0 1 0 7.07"/></svg></button></span></h3>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Corporations utilize information subsidies, such as press releases and media briefings, to shape media narratives around product launches, corporate responsibility initiatives, and regulatory advocacy, thereby reducing journalists' resource demands while advancing commercial interests. A 2017 analysis of 4,455 press releases issued by Dutch organizations over a decade demonstrated that these subsidies directly influenced newspaper and news agency agendas, with organizational releases exhibiting higher media pickup rates when aligned with prominent news values like conflict or prominence.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-5"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-5">[5]</a></sup></a></sup> In the corporate sector specifically, 1,937 press releases were examined, revealing their role in prioritizing business-friendly coverage over less subsidized topics.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-31"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-31">[31]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">A notable case occurred during the 2014 U.S. net neutrality debate, where corporations like Netflix (via CEO Reed Hastings) and Verizon (via CEO Lowell McAdam) acted as key information subsidizers on Twitter, contributing to 29% of industry-sourced content in the top 150 most-retweeted URLs from 6,289 analyzed tweets between February 23 and March 14.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-36"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-36">[36]</a></sup></a></sup> This digital adaptation amplified corporate voices in policy discourse, with network and content providers dominating 21% of citations, often framing arguments to favor market deregulation despite opposition from advocacy groups. Empirical evidence from such efforts underscores corporations' strategic use of subsidies to embed self-serving frames, as seen in higher coverage rates for subsidized corporate crises or innovations compared to independent reporting.</span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) deploy information subsidies, including advocacy reports and event invitations, to elevate issues like humanitarian crises and policy reform, leveraging their perceived moral authority to compete with corporate narratives. In a study of 595 immigration stories across Mexican and U.S. border-state journalism, NGOs ranked as the second-most frequent subsidy source (behind government), with 877 total sources analyzed showing nonprofits' materials shaping  agenda-building on migration flows. Similarly, a 2016 examination highlighted NGOs' use of source credibility—drawing on symbolic capital from partnerships and expertise—as a subsidy to influence policy journalism, such as in European advocacy networks distributing member press releases to secure favorable event coverage.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-8"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-8">[8]</a></sup></a></sup> During the COVID-19 pandemic, NGOs issued targeted subsidies to frame business responses, though their 2,518 press releases in the Dutch study yielded variable uptake, often contingent on alignment with media priorities like urgency.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-37"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-37">[37]</a></sup></a></sup><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-31"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-31">[31]</a></sup></a></sup> These applications enable resource-limited NGOs to amplify underrepresented causes, yet analyses indicate their influence remains secondary to government and corporate subsidies in volume and persistence.</span>
<h2 id="recent-developments-and-future-directions" class="group relative mb-2 mt-5 scroll-mt-24 font-serif text-[1.714286em] font-medium border-border-l1 pb-1 border-b overflow-hidden clear-left">Recent Developments and Future Directions<span class="ml-2 inline-flex items-center gap-1 opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-100"><button type="button" class="heading-copy-link inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-id="recent-developments-and-future-directions" aria-label="Copy link to section" title="Copy link"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"/><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"/></svg></button><button type="button" class="heading-listen inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-section="recent-developments-and-future-directions" aria-label="Listen to this section" title="Listen"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="11 5 6 9 2 9 2 15 6 15 11 19 11 5"/><path d="M15.54 8.46a5 5 0 0 1 0 7.07"/></svg></button></span></h2>
<h3 id="influence-in-digital-and-social-media-eras" class="group relative mb-2 mt-5 scroll-mt-24 font-serif text-[1.428571em] font-medium clear-left">Influence in Digital and Social Media Eras<span class="ml-2 inline-flex items-center gap-1 opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-100"><button type="button" class="heading-copy-link inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-id="influence-in-digital-and-social-media-eras" aria-label="Copy link to section" title="Copy link"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"/><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"/></svg></button><button type="button" class="heading-listen inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-section="influence-in-digital-and-social-media-eras" aria-label="Listen to this section" title="Listen"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="11 5 6 9 2 9 2 15 6 15 11 19 11 5"/><path d="M15.54 8.46a5 5 0 0 1 0 7.07"/></svg></button></span></h3>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">In the digital and social media eras, information subsidies have evolved from traditional press releases to multifaceted digital strategies, enabling sources to bypass journalistic gatekeepers and directly engage audiences. Governments and corporations increasingly deploy optimized content—such as infographics, short videos, and hashtag campaigns—tailored for platforms like Twitter (now X) and Instagram, which amplify reach through algorithms favoring viral, pre-packaged narratives. News organizations have incorporated user-generated content and branded social media posts, reducing production costs while embedding source agendas into feeds. This shift leverages platform dynamics, where subsidies manifest as sponsored influencers or coordinated bot networks, as evidenced by the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal, where micro-targeted political ads served as subsidies influencing voter behavior via Facebook data.</span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Social media's real-time nature has intensified subsidy efficacy, allowing rapid dissemination during events like the 2020 U.S. elections, where the Trump campaign made extensive use of social media posts including memes and clips. Subsidized content on platforms like TikTok often achieves higher engagement rates than organic posts due to algorithmic boosts, but frequently at the cost of factual dilution, with viral political videos containing unverified claims from PR-sourced material. Critics, including scholars like Oscar Gandy, argue this democratizes information flow but entrenches elite biases, as resource-rich actors dominate feeds; for instance, during the COVID-19 pandemic, pharmaceutical firms used subsidized TikTok campaigns shaping public perceptions on vaccines without traditional fact-checking.</span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">The proliferation of subsidies in these eras has prompted regulatory scrutiny, with the European Union's 2022 Digital Services Act mandating transparency for sponsored content to mitigate undue influence. However, enforcement challenges persist, as subsidy-driven misinformation often exploits lax moderation. Defenders highlight efficiency gains, noting that platforms' data analytics enable precise targeting, as seen in corporate sustainability campaigns by firms like Unilever using Instagram reels. Overall, while digital subsidies enhance accessibility, they amplify echo chambers, with data showing increases in polarized content consumption tied to algorithmically promoted subsidies.</span>
<h3 id="applications-in-crises-and-elections-post-2020" class="group relative mb-2 mt-5 scroll-mt-24 font-serif text-[1.428571em] font-medium clear-left">Applications in Crises and Elections Post-2020<span class="ml-2 inline-flex items-center gap-1 opacity-0 transition-opacity group-hover:opacity-100"><button type="button" class="heading-copy-link inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-id="applications-in-crises-and-elections-post-2020" aria-label="Copy link to section" title="Copy link"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"/><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"/></svg></button><button type="button" class="heading-listen inline-flex h-6 w-6 items-center justify-center rounded text-fg-tertiary hover:text-fg-primary hover:bg-surface-l2 transition-colors" data-section="applications-in-crises-and-elections-post-2020" aria-label="Listen to this section" title="Listen"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="11 5 6 9 2 9 2 15 6 15 11 19 11 5"/><path d="M15.54 8.46a5 5 0 0 1 0 7.07"/></svg></button></span></h3>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic's continuation into 2021 and beyond, governments intensified the use of information subsidies to coordinate crisis communication across agencies and media outlets. For instance, Turkey's Ministry of Health positioned itself as a central information subsidy provider via social media, disseminating daily statistics on cases, tests, hospitalizations, and deaths, alongside campaigns like &quot;#LifeFitsIntoHome&quot; launched on March 22, 2020, which promoted social distancing through infographics and videos.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-38"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-38">[38]</a></sup></a></sup> This approach achieved substantial media pickup, with over 633 COVID-19-related Twitter posts garnering millions of engagements, thereby shaping national narratives on prevention and hospital capacities despite criticisms of data accuracy from independent observers.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-38"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-38">[38]</a></sup></a></sup> Similarly, interagency efforts in the United States emphasized social media subsidies during the pandemic's active phases, prioritizing state-level over local sourcing to streamline messaging on mitigation strategies.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-39"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-39">[39]</a></sup></a></sup></span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">The 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine exemplified information subsidies in geopolitical crises, with Ukrainian leadership deploying ready-to-use digital content to influence global media agendas. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's frequent video addresses functioned as &quot;direct video press releases,&quot; providing pre-packaged footage that international outlets adopted with minimal adaptation, facilitating rapid narrative building around Ukrainian resilience and Russian aggression. This strategy aligned with broader nation-branding efforts, where controlled information flows from official sources bypassed traditional verification delays, though it raised questions about media overreliance on state-subsidized content amid conflicting reports from the front lines.</span>
<span data-tts-block="true" class="mb-4 block break-words text-[1em] leading-[1.85]">Post-2020 elections saw political actors adapt information subsidies to digital platforms for agenda building, particularly in the United States. During the 2020 presidential campaign, candidates and parties utilized tweets as novel information subsidies to promote issue salience, with content analysis revealing their role in transferring priorities like economic recovery and pandemic response from campaign agendas to media coverage.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-40"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-40">[40]</a></sup></a></sup> This digital shift persisted into subsequent cycles, as evidenced by comparative studies of election news on platforms like Facebook, where subsidized content from partisan sources influenced visibility and framing, often amplifying polarized topics over neutral reporting.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-41"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-41">[41]</a></sup></a></sup> Empirical tracking indicated that such subsidies competed effectively for attention, though their impact varied by outlet receptivity, underscoring persistent elite influence in resource-constrained news environments.<sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-42"><sup class="text-fg-secondary ml-[2px] cursor-pointer text-xs hover:underline"><a href="#ref-42">[42]</a></sup></a></sup></span>

(function() {
  var btn = document.getElementById('mobile-toc-btn');
  var backdrop = document.getElementById('mobile-toc-backdrop');
  var drawer = document.getElementById('mobile-toc-drawer');
  var closeBtn = document.getElementById('mobile-toc-close');
  if (!btn || !backdrop || !drawer || !closeBtn) return;

  var isOpen = false;
  var headerOffset = 96;

  function open() {
    isOpen = true;
    backdrop.classList.remove('hidden');
    drawer.classList.remove('-translate-x-full');
    drawer.classList.add('translate-x-0');
    document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden';
    syncActiveItem();
  }

  function close() {
    isOpen = false;
    backdrop.classList.add('hidden');
    drawer.classList.add('-translate-x-full');
    drawer.classList.remove('translate-x-0');
    document.body.style.overflow = '';
  }

  // Sync active heading from page's scroll-spy
  function syncActiveItem() {
    var headings = document.querySelectorAll('h1[id], h2[id], h3[id], h4[id], h5[id], h6[id]');
    var threshold = headerOffset + 300;
    var last = null;
    for (var i = 0; i < headings.length; i++) {
      if (headings[i].getBoundingClientRect().top <= threshold) last = headings[i].id;
    }
    var refs = document.getElementById('references');
    if (refs && refs.getBoundingClientRect().top <= threshold) last = 'references';

    var items = document.querySelectorAll('.mobile-toc-item');
    for (var i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
      var item = items[i];
      var dot = item.querySelector('.mobile-toc-dot');
      var link = item.querySelector('.mobile-toc-link');
      var isActive = item.dataset.tocId === last;
      if (dot) dot.style.opacity = isActive ? '1' : '0';
      if (link) {
        link.style.opacity = isActive ? '1' : '0.5';
        link.style.fontWeight = isActive ? '600' : 'normal';
      }
    }
  }

  btn.addEventListener('click', open);
  backdrop.addEventListener('click', close);
  closeBtn.addEventListener('click', close);

  // Handle TOC link clicks
  var links = drawer.querySelectorAll('.mobile-toc-link');
  for (var i = 0; i < links.length; i++) {
    links[i].addEventListener('click', function(e) {
      e.preventDefault();
      var id = this.dataset.tocId;
      var el = document.getElementById(id);
      if (!el) return;
      close();
      // Small delay for drawer close animation
      setTimeout(function() {
        var top = el.getBoundingClientRect().top + window.scrollY - headerOffset;
        window.scrollTo({ top: top });
        history.replaceState(null, '', '#' + id);
      }, 50);
    });
  }

  // Escape key closes drawer
  document.addEventListener('keydown', function(e) {
    if (e.key === 'Escape' && isOpen) close();
  });
})();
</script><button id="scroll-to-top" type="button" class="fixed bottom-4 right-4 z-40 hidden h-10 w-10 items-center justify-center rounded-full border border-border-l1 bg-surface-l1 text-fg-primary shadow-lg transition-opacity duration-200 hover:bg-surface-l2" aria-label="Scroll to top" title="Scroll to top"> <svg class="h-6 w-6 -rotate-90" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" viewBox="0 0 24 24"> <path d="m9 18 6-6-6-6"></path> </svg> </button> <script nonce="3tVkY7j3Vs/FkW2btG+IQg==">
(function() {
  var btn = document.getElementById('scroll-to-top');
  if (!btn) return;

  // Only show on non-mobile (check width)
  var SCROLL_THRESHOLD = 300;
  var visible = false;

  function update() {
    var isMobile = window.innerWidth < 768;
    var shouldShow = !isMobile && window.scrollY > SCROLL_THRESHOLD;

    if (shouldShow && !visible) {
      visible = true;
      btn.style.display = 'flex';
      // Force reflow for transition
      btn.offsetHeight;
      btn.style.opacity = '1';
    } else if (!shouldShow && visible) {
      visible = false;
      btn.style.opacity = '0';
      setTimeout(function() {
        if (!visible) btn.style.display = 'none';
      }, 200);
    }
  }

  btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
    window.scrollTo({ top: 0 });
  });

  window.addEventListener('scroll', update, { passive: true });
  window.addEventListener('resize', update, { passive: true });

  // Initial state
  btn.style.display = 'none';
  btn.style.opacity = '0';
})();
</script><!-- Shared popover container — one for the whole page --><div id="page-popover" role="tooltip" class="pointer-events-none fixed z-50 w-[400px] max-w-[calc(100vw-32px)] rounded-xl border border-border-l1 bg-surface-base p-4 shadow-lg opacity-0 transition-opacity duration-150 dark:bg-surface-l2" style="display:none"> <div id="page-popover-inner"></div> </div> <script nonce="3tVkY7j3Vs/FkW2btG+IQg==">
(function () {
  // ── Config ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  var HOVER_DELAY = 300;   // ms before showing (matches Next.js)
  var CLOSE_DELAY = 200;   // ms grace period when moving to popover
  var CACHE_TTL   = 3600000; // 1 hour (matches Next.js staleTime)
  var MAX_PARA    = 280;     // max chars for first-paragraph excerpt

  // ── DOM refs ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  var popover = document.getElementById('page-popover');
  var inner   = document.getElementById('page-popover-inner');
  if (!popover || !inner) return;

  // ── State ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  var cache      = {};          // slug → { data, ts }
  var inflight   = {};          // slug → Promise
  var hoverTimer = null;
  var closeTimer = null;
  var activeSlug = null;
  var activeLinkEl = null;

  // ── API fetch ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  function fetchPreview(slug) {
    // Return cached if fresh
    var cached = cache[slug];
    if (cached && (Date.now() - cached.ts) < CACHE_TTL) {
      return Promise.resolve(cached.data);
    }
    // Dedupe in-flight
    if (inflight[slug]) return inflight[slug];

    var url = '/api/page-preview?slug=' + encodeURIComponent(slug);
    var p = fetch(url).then(function (res) {
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.status);
      return res.json();
    }).then(function (data) {
      cache[slug] = { data: data, ts: Date.now() };
      delete inflight[slug];
      return data;
    }).catch(function (err) {
      delete inflight[slug];
      return null;
    });

    inflight[slug] = p;
    return p;
  }

  // ── Text extraction helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────
  // These mirror the Next.js extractFirstParagraph + cleanup logic exactly.

  function stripInfobox(content) {
    return content
      .replace(/<!--Infobox Start \[[^\]]+\]-->[\s\S]*?<!--Infobox End-->/g, '')
      .replace(/\n{3,}/g, '\n\n');
  }

  function stripLeadingImage(content) {
    var cleaned = content.replace(/^\s*!\[[^\]]*\]\([^)]+\)\s*/m, '');
    return cleaned.replace(/^\s*\*[^*]+\*\s*/m, '');
  }

  function isListItem(line) {
    if (/^[*-]\s/.test(line)) return true;
    if (/^\d+\.\s/.test(line)) return true;
    return false;
  }

  function extractFirstParagraph(content) {
    if (!content) return '';
    var clean = stripInfobox(content);
    clean = stripLeadingImage(clean);
    var lines = clean.split('\n');
    var para = '';
    var inPara = false;

    for (var i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) {
      var t = lines[i].trim();
      if (!t && !inPara) continue;
      if (t.indexOf('<!--') === 0 || t.indexOf('-->') === t.length - 3) continue;
      if (
        t.charAt(0) === '#' || t.indexOf('![') === 0 || t.charAt(0) === '|' ||
        t.charAt(0) === '>' || t.indexOf('```') === 0 ||
        t.indexOf('<grok-render') === 0 || isListItem(t)
      ) {
        if (inPara && para) break;
        continue;
      }
      if (!t && inPara) break;
      if (t) { inPara = true; para += (para ? ' ' : '') + t; }
    }

    // Clean markdown artefacts
    para = para
      .replace(/<grok-render[^>]*\/>/g, '')
      .replace(/\[([^\]]+)\]\([^)]+\)/g, '$1')
      .replace(/\[\]/g, '')
      .replace(/\(https?:\/\/[^)]+\)/g, '')
      .replace(/https?:\/\/\S+/g, '')
      .replace(/\*\*([^*]+)\*\*/g, '$1')
      .replace(/\*([^*]+)\*/g, '$1')
      .replace(/__([^_]+)__/g, '$1')
      .replace(/_([^_]+)_/g, '$1')
      .replace(/`([^`]+)`/g, '$1')
      .replace(/\s+/g, ' ')
      .trim();

    if (para.length > MAX_PARA) para = para.slice(0, MAX_PARA - 3) + '...';
    return para;
  }

  // ── Image extraction ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  function extractLeadingImage(content) {
    if (!content) return null;
    var withoutInfobox = stripInfobox(content);
    // Find first H1, take body after it
    var h1Match = withoutInfobox.match(/^(#\s+.+)$/m);
    var body = h1Match
      ? withoutInfobox.slice(withoutInfobox.indexOf(h1Match[1]) + h1Match[1].length).replace(/^\n+/, '')
      : withoutInfobox;
    var imgMatch = body.match(/^\s*!\[[^\]]*\]\(([^\s")]+)(?:\s+"[^"]*")?\)/);
    if (!imgMatch) return null;
    return getControlledImageUrl(imgMatch[1]);
  }

  function getControlledImageUrl(src) {
    if (!src) return null;
    if (src.indexOf('./_assets_/') === 0 || src.indexOf('._assets_/') === 0) return null;
    if (src.indexOf('http://') === 0 || src.indexOf('https://') === 0) {
      try {
        var u = new URL(src);
        if (u.hostname === 'assets.grokipedia.com') return src;
      } catch (e) {}
      return null;
    }
    return null;
  }

  // ── Render popover content ──────────────────────────────────────────
  function renderLoading() {
    return '<div class="flex h-16 items-center justify-center">' +
      '<div class="h-5 w-5 animate-spin rounded-full border-2 border-t-transparent" ' +
      'style="border-color:hsl(var(--fg-secondary));border-top-color:transparent"></div></div>';
  }

  function renderNotFound() {
    return '<p class="text-sm" style="color:hsl(var(--fg-secondary))">Article not found</p>';
  }

  function renderPreview(page) {
    var imageUrl = extractLeadingImage(page.content || '');
    var paragraph = extractFirstParagraph(page.content || page.description || '');
    var html = '<div class="flex flex-col gap-3">';

    if (imageUrl) {
      html += '<div class="w-full overflow-hidden rounded-lg">' +
        '<img src="' + escapeAttr(imageUrl) + '" alt="' + escapeAttr(page.title || '') +
        '" class="h-auto max-h-[200px] w-full object-cover" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" ' +
        'loading="eager" decoding="async" onerror="this.parentElement.style.display=\'none\'" />' +
        '</div>';
    }

    html += '<div class="flex flex-col gap-1">';
    html += '<h3 class="font-serif text-base font-semibold leading-tight" style="color:hsl(var(--fg-primary))">' +
      escapeHtml(page.title || '') + '</h3>';
    if (paragraph) {
      html += '<p class="line-clamp-4 text-sm leading-relaxed" style="color:hsl(var(--fg-secondary))">' +
        escapeHtml(paragraph) + '</p>';
    }
    html += '</div></div>';
    return html;
  }

  function escapeHtml(s) {
    return s.replace(/&/g, '&amp;').replace(/</g, '&lt;').replace(/>/g, '&gt;').replace(/"/g, '&quot;');
  }
  function escapeAttr(s) { return escapeHtml(s); }

  // ── Positioning ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  function positionPopover(linkEl) {
    var rect = linkEl.getBoundingClientRect();
    var gap = 8;
    var pw = 400;
    var vw = window.innerWidth;
    var vh = window.innerHeight;

    // Ensure visible for measurement (but don't move off-screen — that
    // triggers mouseleave on the popover and causes the close race).
    popover.style.display = 'block';
    var ph = popover.offsetHeight || 200;

    // Horizontal: prefer left-aligned with link, clamp to viewport
    var left = rect.left;
    if (left + pw > vw - 16) left = vw - pw - 16;
    if (left < 16) left = 16;

    // Vertical: prefer below, flip above if no room
    var top;
    if (rect.bottom + gap + ph <= vh) {
      top = rect.bottom + gap;
    } else if (rect.top - gap - ph >= 0) {
      top = rect.top - gap - ph;
    } else {
      top = Math.max(16, vh - ph - 16);
    }

    popover.style.left = left + 'px';
    popover.style.top  = top + 'px';
  }

  // ── Show / Hide ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  function showPopover(slug, linkEl) {
    // Cancel any pending hide from a previous hover
    if (hideTimer) { clearTimeout(hideTimer); hideTimer = null; }

    activeSlug = slug;
    activeLinkEl = linkEl;
    popover.classList.add('pointer-events-auto');
    popover.classList.remove('pointer-events-none');

    // Show loading state immediately
    inner.innerHTML = renderLoading();
    positionPopover(linkEl);
    popover.style.opacity = '1';

    fetchPreview(slug).then(function (data) {
      // Bail if user already moved away
      if (activeSlug !== slug) return;
      if (!data || !data.found || !data.page) {
        inner.innerHTML = renderNotFound();
      } else {
        inner.innerHTML = renderPreview(data.page);
      }
      // Reposition after content changes height
      positionPopover(linkEl);
    });
  }

  var hideTimer = null;

  function hidePopover() {
    activeSlug = null;
    activeLinkEl = null;
    popover.style.opacity = '0';
    popover.classList.remove('pointer-events-auto');
    popover.classList.add('pointer-events-none');
    // Hide after fade-out transition — but cancel if re-shown
    if (hideTimer) clearTimeout(hideTimer);
    hideTimer = setTimeout(function () {
      hideTimer = null;
      if (!activeSlug) popover.style.display = 'none';
    }, 200);
  }

  // ── Slug extraction ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  function getSlugFromLink(el) {
    var href = el.getAttribute('href');
    if (!href) return null;
    var match = href.match(/^\/page\/(.+)$/);
    return match ? decodeURIComponent(match[1]) : null;
  }

  function findPageLink(target) {
    var el = target;
    // Walk up at most 5 levels (link might wrap <em>/<strong>/etc.)
    for (var i = 0; i < 5 && el && el !== document.body; i++) {
      if (el.tagName === 'A' && el.getAttribute('href') && el.getAttribute('href').indexOf('/page/') === 0) {
        return el;
      }
      el = el.parentElement;
    }
    return null;
  }

  // ── Event delegation on article ─────────────────────────────────────
  var article = document.querySelector('article');
  if (!article) return;

  article.addEventListener('mouseenter', function (e) {
    var linkEl = findPageLink(e.target);
    if (!linkEl) return;

    // Ignore if the pointer came from another element inside the same link
    // (just moving between child elements — not a real entry)
    if (e.relatedTarget && linkEl.contains(e.relatedTarget)) return;

    var slug = getSlugFromLink(linkEl);
    if (!slug) return;

    // Cancel any pending close
    if (closeTimer) { clearTimeout(closeTimer); closeTimer = null; }

    // If already showing this slug, keep it
    if (activeSlug === slug) return;

    // Start prefetching immediately
    fetchPreview(slug);

    // Delay showing the popover
    if (hoverTimer) clearTimeout(hoverTimer);
    hoverTimer = setTimeout(function () {
      hoverTimer = null;
      showPopover(slug, linkEl);
    }, HOVER_DELAY);
  }, true);

  article.addEventListener('mouseleave', function (e) {
    var linkEl = findPageLink(e.target);
    if (!linkEl) return;

    // Ignore if the pointer moved to another element still inside the same
    // link — this is just child-to-child movement, not a real leave.
    if (e.relatedTarget && linkEl.contains(e.relatedTarget)) return;

    scheduleClose();
  }, true);

  // ── Popover mouse handling ──────────────────────────────────────────
  popover.addEventListener('mouseenter', function () {
    if (closeTimer) { clearTimeout(closeTimer); closeTimer = null; }
  });

  popover.addEventListener('mouseleave', function () {
    scheduleClose();
  });

  function scheduleClose() {
    if (hoverTimer) { clearTimeout(hoverTimer); hoverTimer = null; }
    if (closeTimer) clearTimeout(closeTimer);
    closeTimer = setTimeout(function () {
      closeTimer = null;
      hidePopover();
    }, CLOSE_DELAY);
  }

  // ── Touch devices: skip entirely ───────────────────────────────────
  // On touch devices links just navigate — no popover overhead.

  // ── Scroll: reposition if visible ──────────────────────────────────
  var scrollRaf = null;
  window.addEventListener('scroll', function () {
    if (!activeSlug || !activeLinkEl) return;
    if (scrollRaf) return;
    scrollRaf = requestAnimationFrame(function () {
      scrollRaf = null;
      if (activeSlug && activeLinkEl) positionPopover(activeLinkEl);
    });
  }, { passive: true });

  // ── Hide on Escape ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  document.addEventListener('keydown', function (e) {
    if (e.key === 'Escape' && activeSlug) hidePopover();

    }

    function renderEditCard(edit) {

    (function(){

      var submitAnotherBtn = modal.querySelector('[data-submit-another]');

      var editContext = { originalContent: '', sectionTitle: '', editStartHeader: '', editEndHeader: '' };

      function setMode(mode) {

        tabBtns.forEach(function(btn) {

          btn.classList.toggle('bg-surface-base', isActive);
          btn.classList.toggle('text-fg-primary', isActive);
          btn.classList.toggle('shadow-sm', isActive);
          btn.classList.toggle('text-fg-tertiary', !isActive);
        });
        articleForm.classList.toggle('hidden', mode !== 'article');
        editForm.classList.toggle('hidden', mode !== 'edit');
        successState.classList.add('hidden');

        descEl.textContent = mode === 'article'

        titleEl.classList.add('hidden');

        var defaultMsg = currentMode === 'edit'

        })
        .catch(function() {
          showErrorState("Network error. Please check your connection and try again.");
        });
      });

      editForm.addEventListener('submit', function(e) {
        e.preventDefault();
        var summary = editSummary.value.trim();
        if (!summary || !pageSlug) return;
        if(window.__ev)window.__ev('edit_submit', pageSlug);
        editSubmit.disabled = true;
        editSubmit.textContent = 'Submitting…';
        statusEl.classList.add('hidden');

        var evidence = [];
        editEvidenceList.querySelectorAll('[data-edit-evidence]').forEach(function(inp) {
          var url = inp.value.trim();
          if (url) evidence.push({ url: url });
        });

        fetch('/api/create-edit-request', {
          method: 'POST',
          headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
          credentials: 'same-origin',
          body: JSON.stringify({
            slug: pageSlug,
            type: 1,
            summary: summary,
            originalContent: editContext.originalContent,
            proposedContent: editProposed.value.trim(),
            sectionTitle: editContext.sectionTitle,
            editStartHeader: editContext.editStartHeader,
            editEndHeader: editContext.editEndHeader,
            supportingEvidence: evidence,
          })
        })
        .then(function(r) { return r.json().then(function(d) { return { ok: r.ok, data: d }; }); })
        .then(function(res) {
          if (res.ok && res.data.success) {
            showSuccessState();
          } else {
            showErrorState(res.data.error || "We couldn't submit your edit. Please try again.");
          }
        })
        .catch(function() {
          showErrorState("Network error. Please check your connection and try again.");
        });
      });
    })();
    </script> </body> </html>
